treaty_name: Treaty with the Delawares (Fort Pitt)
nations: Delaware (Lenape)
mechanism_summary: Fort Pitt 1778: first U.S.-Indian treaty and the Delaware (Lenape) statehood clause -- Article VI of the 1778 treaty guaranteed the Delawares their territorial rights within earlier boundaries while friendship held, and contemplated a Delaware-headed state with representation in Congress, but only if Congress approved. Congress never approved the state; the guaranteed boundaries were then given up through successive cessions and removals (Greenville 1795, later Ohio/Indiana cessions, and the 1866 Kansas treaty that arranged sale of the Delaware reserve to railroad interests and removal to Indian Territory). Read the statehood clause as a conditional proposal that lapsed, not as a binding promise that was 'broken'; the territorial guarantee is the stronger breach claim.
land_lost_description: Delaware homelands in the Ohio country, then Indiana, then the Kansas reserve; ultimate relocation to Indian Territory.
legal_aftermath: No general Delaware claim of record verified this session. Later Delaware cessions and the 1866 sale terms are documented in the treaty texts.

treaty_name: Treaty of Hopewell (7 Stat. 18); Treaty of Holston
nations: Cherokee
mechanism_summary: Hopewell 1785 and Holston 1791: settler intrusion onto Cherokee land -- The 1785 treaty stated 'No citizen of the United States shall settle on Indian lands.' Roughly 3,000 settlers of the unrecognized State of Franklin already occupied Cherokee land between the Holston and French Broad rivers; the Confederation government did not remove them. Franklin made its own treaties with the Cherokee (Dumplin Creek 1785, Coyatee 1786), which the United States did not recognize. The dispute continued until Holston (1791) set a new border.
land_lost_description: Land between the Holston and French Broad rivers in present-day Tennessee, and a wedge near the Cumberland (Nashville).
legal_aftermath: No court remedy. The boundary was reset by a new treaty (Holston 1791), i.e., the loss was ratified rather than reversed.

treaty_name: Treaty of Fort Stanwix
nations: Haudenosaunee (Six Nations); Seneca, Cayuga, Onondaga, Mohawk, Oneida, Tuscarora
mechanism_summary: Fort Stanwix 1784: cession by Haudenosaunee delegates who lacked authority -- Signed after the Revolutionary War by Haudenosaunee representatives (Brant left early; Cornerplanter and Aaron Hill signed). The Six Nations council at Buffalo Creek refused to ratify, arguing its delegates had no authority to give away such large tracts, and asked for the deeds back. The United States renewed its claims in the Treaty of Fort Harmar (1789). This is a contested-authority/duress problem, not a statute-based abrogation.
land_lost_description: Claims to the Ohio country, a strip along the Niagara River, and land west of Buffalo Creek (Pennsylvania 'Last Purchase').
legal_aftermath: Treated by the United States as valid; no court remedy. Later Haudenosaunee land claims in New York rest on the Nonintercourse Act rather than on Stanwix (see V018).

treaty_name: Treaty of Greenville (7 Stat. 49); Treaty of Fort Wayne
nations: Shawnee; Wyandot, Delaware, Ottawa, Chippewa, Potawatomi, Miami, Eel River, Wea, Kickapoo, Piankeshaw, Kaskaskia
mechanism_summary: Greenville 1795 and Fort Wayne 1809: encroachment, then cession under pressure -- Greenville (Aug. 3, 1795; Senate ratified Dec. 22, 1795) ceded about two-thirds of the Ohio country in exchange for annuities. Settlers kept crossing the treaty line, especially in Indiana, and the Army did not enforce it. The 1809 Fort Wayne treaty (Delaware, Potawatomi, Miami, Eel River) pushed the line further; Tecumseh, who had not signed Greenville, rebuilt the confederacy at Prophetstown in response. Fort Wayne's acreage and the claim that Miami/Shawnee interests were bypassed are standard in the literature but were not confirmed in sources read.
land_lost_description: Ohio (about two-thirds) in 1795; further Indiana land in 1809.
acreage_if_known: Fort Wayne 1809 commonly given as roughly 2.5-3 million acres [from-memory; unverified]
legal_aftermath: No claim of record. Military outcome: Tippecanoe (1811), War of 1812.

treaty_name: Treaty of St. Louis (Sauk and Fox)
nations: Sauk (Sac) and Meskwaki (Fox)
mechanism_summary: Treaty of St. Louis 1804: cession signed by a delegation with no authority to sell -- Sauk hunters killed four settlers in 1804; a delegation went to St. Louis to resolve the killings (not to sell land). Under William Henry Harrison they signed a cession of a large area between the Mississippi and Illinois rivers, including the Rock River villages, for goods worth $2,234.50 plus a $1,000 annuity. The delegation lacked authority under Sauk and Meskwaki custom; Black Hawk wrote the delegates were drunk much of the time. Portage des Sioux (1815) upheld the treaty; Black Hawk's resistance became the 1832 Black Hawk War.
land_lost_description: Rock River valley and a large area of NW Illinois, S Wisconsin and NE Missouri.
acreage_if_known: 'about 51 million acres' appears in the literature [from-memory; not in source read]
legal_aftermath: No remedy; Sauk and Fox later removed west. Tribal governments: Sac & Fox Nation, Sac & Fox Tribe of the Mississippi in Iowa (Meskwaki), Sac & Fox of Missouri.

treaty_name: Treaty with the Cherokee (New Echota)
nations: Cherokee
mechanism_summary: Treaty of New Echota (1835) and the Trail of Tears (1838-39) -- Signed Dec. 29, 1835 by a minority 'Treaty Party' (Major Ridge, Elias Boudinot, John Ridge) without authorization from the Cherokee government under Principal Chief John Ross. Ross presented petitions against it with thousands of Cherokee names (sources give 13,000 to almost 16,000; one National Archives-linked item counts 3,352 signatures on one petition). The Senate ratified in May 1836 by a single vote; proclaimed May 23, 1836 (7 Stat. 478). General Winfield Scott began enforcing removal in May 1838 with about 7,000 troops and militia. Removal ran Oct. 1838-Mar. 1839. Article 7 promised a Cherokee delegate in the House 'once Congress makes provision'; no delegate has been seated.
land_lost_description: All Cherokee lands east of the Mississippi for $5 million, in exchange for land in Indian Territory (the treaty also adds a tract estimated at 800,000 acres).
acreage_if_known: Cession had no stated acreage; Georgia/Tennessee/Alabama/North Carolina homeland. West: 7 million acres plus 800,000-acre tract (per treaty).
legal_aftermath: Cherokee Nation v. Georgia (1831); Worcester v. Georgia (1832) held Georgia's laws void in Cherokee territory. Death toll estimates: about 4,000 (most cited; Elizur Butler), range 2,000-6,000 (secondary). Cherokee Nation (2019-) has pressed Article 7 delegate seat (Kimberly Teehee); outcome beyond 2022 not verified.
related_cases: Cherokee Nation v. Georgia, 30 U.S. (5 Pet.) 1 (1831); Worcester v. Georgia, 31 U.S. (6 Pet.) 515 (1832)

treaty_name: Treaties of Hopewell (1785) and Holston (1791) as read in Worcester
nations: Cherokee
mechanism_summary: Georgia ignores Worcester v. Georgia (1832): the federal government declines to enforce -- After Georgia extended its laws over the Cherokee Nation (1828-30, following the discovery of gold near Dahlonega in 1828), the Supreme Court held in Worcester (Mar. 3, 1832) that Georgia's laws had no force in Cherokee territory and that missionary Samuel Worcester's conviction was void. The executive branch did not enforce the decision. The remark attributed to Andrew Jackson ('John Marshall has made his decision; now let him enforce it') is probably apocryphal.
land_lost_description: Practical protection of the Cherokee Nation's territorial integrity; precondition for the New Echota minority treaty (V006) and removal.
legal_aftermath: Worcester remains good law on the point that states lack authority in Indian country absent federal consent, but its force was narrowed in Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta (2022); see V048.
related_cases: Worcester v. Georgia, 31 U.S. (6 Pet.) 515 (1832); Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta, 597 U.S. ___ (2022)

treaty_name: Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek
nations: Choctaw
mechanism_summary: Dancing Rabbit Creek 1830: first removal treaty under the Indian Removal Act -- Concluded Sept. 27, 1830 (7 Stat. 333), proclaimed Feb. 24, 1831. The Choctaw ceded about 11 million acres of Mississippi for about 15 million acres in Indian Territory. Article 14 offered 640-acre allotments (and smaller amounts for children) to heads of family who stayed and accepted U.S. citizenship. About 15,000 Choctaw plus roughly 1,000 enslaved people were moved in three migrations (1831-33); about 2,500 died. Those who stayed (5,000-6,000) faced years of legal conflict, harassment and intimidation; the Article 14 promise did not protect their land in practice.
land_lost_description: About 11 million acres in Mississippi.
acreage_if_known: about 11 million acres ceded; about 15 million received in the West
legal_aftermath: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians reorganized and gained federal recognition in 1945. The Choctaw Nation in Oklahoma lost its government under the Curtis Act (1898); see V044.

treaty_name: Treaty of Payne's Landing (7 Stat. 368); Moultrie Creek (1823)
nations: Seminole
mechanism_summary: Seminole removal: Payne's Landing (1832), Fort Gibson (1833) and the Second Seminole War -- Moultrie Creek (1823) gave the Seminole a central Florida reservation with guaranteed U.S. services for 20 years. Payne's Landing (May 9, 1832) said the Seminole would move west if the land proved suitable, within three years; the Senate ratified in April 1834. In March 1833 seven inspecting chiefs signed a statement at Fort Gibson accepting western land; most chiefs later repudiated it as unauthorized or coerced, and five leading chiefs including Micanopy had refused removal. The Second Seminole War (1835-42) followed; by 1842, 3,612 Seminole had relocated; 350-500 remained in Florida, and a Third Seminole War (1855-58) pressed most of the rest west. No peace treaty ended the Second War.
land_lost_description: Florida reservation lands; population divided between Indian Territory and Florida.
legal_aftermath: Seminole Nation v. United States (1942) imposed strict fiduciary standards on payments to the Nation (see V043). Seminole Tribe of Florida regards the wars as one continuous conflict (secondary).
related_cases: Seminole Nation v. United States, 316 U.S. 286 (1942)

treaty_name: Treaty with the Creeks (14 Stat. 785)
nations: Muscogee (Creek) Nation
mechanism_summary: Creek (Muscogee) 1866: punitive cession of the western half of the Nation -- Concluded June 14, 1866; ratified July 19; proclaimed Aug. 11. The preamble recites that the Creek treaty with the Confederate States (1861) left the Nation liable to forfeit benefits under earlier U.S. treaties. Article 3 required the Creeks to cede 'the west half of their entire domain,' estimated at 3,250,560 acres priced at 30 cents per acre ($975,168), to settle other Indians as the U.S. chose. This is a coerced cession imposed as a condition of restored relations (similar terms were imposed on the Seminole, Cherokee, Choctaw and Chickasaw in 1866).
land_lost_description: West half of the Creek domain.
legal_aftermath: The remaining Creek land is the territory at issue in McGirt (2020), where the Court read the 1866 treaty as 'forever set apart' land and held the reservation never disestablished (see V047).
related_cases: McGirt v. Oklahoma, 591 U.S. ___ (2020)

treaty_name: Treaty of Yellow River (1836); Treaty of Tippecanoe (1832)
nations: Potawatomi (Menominee band, Twin Lakes)
mechanism_summary: Potawatomi Trail of Death (1838) and the disputed Yellow River treaty (1836) -- The 1832 Tippecanoe treaty reserved 22 sections (14,080 acres) for Chief Menominee and associated bands. The Aug. 5, 1836 Yellow River treaty ceded the reserve and required removal within two years; Menominee and 17 band members refused to recognize it and protested forged signatures. On Aug. 30, 1838, Gen. John Tipton's volunteer militia surrounded the Twin Lakes village after a council call. The march began Sept. 4 with 859 people and ran about 660 miles in 61 days to near Osawatomie, Kansas; 42 died, 28 of them children.
land_lost_description: Reserve of 14,080 acres in Indiana and the Twin Lakes village.
legal_aftermath: No remedy located. Potawatomi nations (Citizen Potawatomi, Prairie Band, Forest County, Pokagon, Hannahville, Match-e-be-nash-she-wish) hold the remembrance.

treaty_name: Treaty of Buffalo Creek (1838); Treaty with the Seneca (1842); Treaty with the Tonawanda Band (1857)
nations: Seneca Nation (Seneca Nation of Indians) and Tonawanda Band of Seneca; other New York nations
mechanism_summary: Treaty of Buffalo Creek (1838): sale of Seneca reservations and the 1842 and 1857 corrections -- The Jan. 15, 1838 treaty, signed by the U.S. and nine New York nations as part of the removal program, acknowledged that the Ogden Land Company would buy the four remaining Seneca reservations in New York, with proceeds to fund removal to Kansas Territory. The Tonawanda Seneca said they were not consulted and that their chiefs did not sign; they refused to leave. A 1842 treaty modified the 1838 agreement: the Ogden Company had bought only two reservations (including Tonawanda), and the Seneca kept Cattaraugus and Allegany. In 1857 the Tonawanda Band's separate treaty let it use its share of the earlier sale to repurchase most of its reservation.
land_lost_description: Buffalo Creek reservation (and, until 1857, most of Tonawanda). Allegany and Cattaraugus retained.
legal_aftermath: Corrected only by new treaties (1842, 1857). Widely reported allegations of bribery and forged consent, and the Senate's narrow ratification margin, were not confirmed in sources read.

treaty_name: Treaty with the Chippewa (1837, 7 Stat. 536); 1842 treaty
nations: Ojibwe (Anishinaabe), Lake Superior and Mississippi bands
mechanism_summary: Sandy Lake (1850): removal order and annuity relocation in breach of Ojibwe treaties -- Taylor-administration and Minnesota Territory officials (Ewing, Brown, Ramsey, Watrous) sought to move several Ojibwe bands west of the Mississippi. The fall annuity payment was moved from La Pointe, Wisconsin, to Sandy Lake, Minnesota, to strand the bands through winter. Nearly 3,000 men waited weeks; only part of the payment arrived and much food had spoiled. About 150 died at Sandy Lake and 200 to 230 more on the way home; about 400 total (roughly 12% of the people per one source). Chief Buffalo of La Pointe lobbied President Fillmore to cancel the order, leading to the 1854 treaty and permanent reservations. Article 5 of the 1837 treaty protected hunting, fishing and wild-rice gathering 'during the pleasure of the President'.
land_lost_description: Lives; security of residence in ceded territory; leverage that was converted into the 1854 reservation system.
legal_aftermath: The 1850 order's treaty-rights revocation was held ineffective in Mille Lacs (1999), see V014. No compensation for the Sandy Lake deaths located.
related_cases: Minnesota v. Mille Lacs Band, 526 U.S. 172 (1999)

treaty_name: Treaty with the Chippewa (1837), 7 Stat. 536
nations: Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe (Chippewa)
mechanism_summary: Mille Lacs (1999): Minnesota's denial of 1837 hunting, fishing and gathering rights -- The 1837 treaty ceded land but kept the 'privilege of hunting, fishing, and gathering the wild rice' on ceded land 'during the pleasure of the President.' An 1850 executive order attempted to revoke the privilege and order removal; the 1855 treaty ceded more land but did not mention the rights; Minnesota became a state in 1858. Minnesota argued each ended the rights. The Supreme Court (5-4, O'Connor) held the 1850 order ineffective (the removal portion lacked legal authority and was not severable), the 1855 treaty did not abrogate the rights, and statehood did not extinguish them.
land_lost_description: (Recovered, not lost) Rights had been denied in practice by state regulation until the ruling.
legal_aftermath: Rights confirmed. Counterexample of treaty-rights vindication; shows that abrogation requires clear congressional intent.
related_cases: Minnesota v. Mille Lacs Band of Chippewa Indians, 526 U.S. 172 (1999); Herrera v. Wyoming, 587 U.S. ___ (2019)

nations: Lac Courte Oreilles, Bad River, Red Cliff, Lac du Flambeau, St. Croix, Sokaogon (Mole Lake) Ojibwe
mechanism_summary: Voigt decision (1983): Wisconsin's denial of 1837/1842 treaty rights -- Wisconsin prosecuted Ojibwe members for off-reservation fishing and hunting in ceded territory. Lac Courte Oreilles v. Voigt (7th Cir. 1983) is the leading decision that the 1837 and 1842 treaties preserved those rights; spearfishing disputes escalated through 1989. GLIFWC (created 1984) co-manages the treaty-ceded territories for 11 Ojibwe nations.
land_lost_description: (Rights asserted and later confirmed.)
legal_aftermath: Rights confirmed; GLIFWC established 1984.
related_cases: Lac Courte Oreilles Band v. Voigt, 700 F.2d 341 (7th Cir. 1983) [from-memory citation]

treaty_name: Treaty of Wolf River (1854)
nations: Menominee Indian Tribe of Wisconsin
mechanism_summary: Menominee termination (1954-1973) -- The 1854 treaty assigned the Menominee a Wolf River reservation (432 sq mi per one source; about 235,000 acres per an 1870 assessment). The Menominee Termination Act (Pub. L. 399, 68 Stat. 250, 1954) provided for a per capita distribution of tribal funds and 'orderly termination of Federal supervision.' Termination took effect April 30, 1961; the reservation became Menominee County. A 1968 Supreme Court decision (Menominee Tribe v. United States) held that treaty hunting and fishing rights survived termination because Congress did not clearly abrogate them. After organizing by DRUMS (1970), the Menominee Restoration Act (Pub. L. 93-197, 87 Stat. 770, Dec. 22, 1973) restored federal recognition; the reservation was re-established in 1975.
land_lost_description: Federal recognition and trust status (1961-1973); county-form governance; enterprise and land-sale pressures.
legal_aftermath: Menominee Tribe v. United States (1968) preserved treaty hunting/fishing rights; Restoration Act 1973. One of the few full restorations of land and status.
related_cases: Menominee Tribe of Indians v. United States, 391 U.S. 404 (1968)

treaty_name: Treaty with the Six Nations (Canandaigua), 7 Stat. 44
nations: Seneca Nation of Indians (Allegany Reservation); Haudenosaunee
mechanism_summary: Canandaigua 1794 and the Kinzua Dam (1958-1965) -- Article 3 of the treaty (concluded Nov. 11, 1794; proclaimed Jan. 21, 1795) acknowledged Seneca land and says the United States 'will never claim the same,' for the Seneca's 'free use and enjoyment.' Congress authorized the Allegheny Reservoir/Kinzua Dam under Flood Control Acts of 1936 and 1938 and appropriated for it in 1957. The Seneca challenged it as a violation of the 1794 treaty; the D.C. Circuit (Nov. 25, 1958) held Congress may authorize a taking of treaty-protected land by eminent domain if it clearly shows that intent, and found it had. The Corps broke ground Oct. 22, 1960; the dam was completed in 1965, filling to 1967. About 10,000 acres (nearly a third of the Allegany Reservation) were flooded and about 600 Seneca were relocated; hundreds of graves were exhumed. An alternative design by engineer Arthur E. Morgan was rejected by the Corps. A 1964 act provided relocation and rehabilitation funds.
land_lost_description: About 10,000 acres of the Allegany Reservation, nine communities.
acreage_if_known: about 10,000 acres; about 600 people (some sources say more than 600 families)
legal_aftermath: No injunction. Compensation by a 1964 act (amount not confirmed this session; commonly reported as $15 million [from-memory]). In March 2026 the Seneca Nation and the Army Corps signed a consultation MOU as the Corps studies dam safety modifications.
related_cases: Seneca Nation of Indians v. Brucker, 262 F.2d 27 (D.C. Cir. 1958), cert. denied (1959) [from-memory on cert]

treaty_name: Treaty of Fort Stanwix (1784), Treaty of Canandaigua (1794), Nonintercourse Act (1790/1793/1834)
nations: Oneida Indian Nation; Haudenosaunee
mechanism_summary: Oneida land (New York): 1795 sale without federal approval -- New York began its own treaties with the Oneida, Tuscarora, Onondaga and Cayuga less than a year after the 1784 Fort Stanwix treaty, arguing it could do so because they lived within the state. The Nonintercourse Act barred sales of Indian land to states or individuals without federal approval. The Court held in County of Oneida v. Oneida Indian Nation (1985) that the Oneida had a federal common-law right to sue over the 1795 conveyance and that no state statute of limitations applied. In City of Sherrill v. Oneida Indian Nation (2005), 8-1, the Court held that the Nation could not revive sovereignty over parcels it had repurchased on the open market, citing laches, acquiescence and impossibility, and pointed to the trust-acquisition process.
land_lost_description: Most of the Oneida homeland in central New York; sovereignty over reacquired parcels (Sherrill).
acreage_if_known: not stated in sources read (reservation was once millions of acres; unverified)
legal_aftermath: Liability for the 1795 sale confirmed (1985); remedies narrowed by Sherrill (2005). Land claims in New York are now largely settled or settlement-driven; details not verified this session.
related_cases: County of Oneida v. Oneida Indian Nation, 470 U.S. 226 (1985); City of Sherrill v. Oneida Indian Nation, 544 U.S. 197 (2005)

treaty_name: Treaty of Canandaigua (1794) invoked; Tuscarora title held in fee
nations: Tuscarora Nation (Haudenosaunee)
mechanism_summary: Tuscarora and the Niagara Power Project (1960) -- The Federal Power Commission licensed New York's Power Authority to build the Niagara reservoir, which required Tuscarora land. The Supreme Court (Mar. 7, 1960) held that land owned in fee simple by the Nation is not a 'reservation' under the Federal Power Act because the United States holds no interest in it, and that Section 21 of the Act lets licensees condemn Indian-owned land with just compensation; neither 25 U.S.C. 177 nor any treaty barred the taking. Three Justices dissented (Black, Warren, Douglas).
land_lost_description: Tuscarora land taken for the reservoir.
legal_aftermath: Takings upheld with compensation. Shows how the form of title (fee vs. trust) and licensee condemnation authority can defeat treaty arguments.
related_cases: Federal Power Commission v. Tuscarora Indian Nation, 362 U.S. 99 (1960)

treaty_name: Treaty of Fort Laramie (Horse Creek), 11 Stat. 749
nations: Cheyenne, Arapaho, Lakota (Sioux), Crow, Assiniboine, Gros Ventre, Mandan, Hidatsa, Arikara
mechanism_summary: Fort Laramie 1851: Pike's Peak gold rush invades treaty territory -- Signed Sept. 17, 1851 at Horse Creek, near Fort Laramie. In Article 3 the United States agreed to protect the nations against depredations by U.S. citizens; Article 5 set each nation's territory (the Cheyenne and Arapaho held a shared area south of the North Platte, mainly in present Wyoming and Colorado). The Senate ratified with an amendment cutting the annuity term (Article 7) from fifty years to ten. The 1858 Pike's Peak gold rush brought miners and settlers into Colorado over tribal protests, and the government did not enforce the treaty. Denver was founded in that territory. The Cheyenne and Arapaho were then pressed into the Fort Wise cession (V021).
land_lost_description: Cheyenne-Arapaho treaty territory in Colorado.
acreage_if_known: not stated in sources read (an unverified secondary figure of nearly 12 million acres across five states exists for the whole treaty)
legal_aftermath: No contemporaneous remedy. 1868 Fort Laramie (V024) later redrew boundaries for the Lakota.

treaty_name: Treaty of Fort Wise, 12 Stat. 1163; Treaty of the Little Arkansas, 14 Stat. 703
nations: Southern Cheyenne and Arapaho (Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes of Oklahoma); Northern Cheyenne descendants
mechanism_summary: Fort Wise (1861), Sand Creek (1864) and the Little Arkansas reparations (1865) -- Fort Wise (signed Feb. 18, 1861; ratified with amendment; proclaimed Dec. 5, 1861) ceded most of the 1851 treaty lands except a reserve on the Arkansas, with $450,000 in annuities over 15 years; Wikipedia states the treaty never had the approval of the Council of 44 (disputed authority). On Nov. 29, 1864, Col. John Chivington's Colorado volunteers attacked a Cheyenne and Arapaho village at Sand Creek; estimates run 70 to over 600 killed, most commonly about 150, about two-thirds women and children. Two military inquiries and a congressional joint committee condemned Chivington; no one was prosecuted. In the Little Arkansas treaty (Oct. 14, 1865), Article VI condemned the attack and promised 320 acres each to four chiefs and 160 acres to each widowed or orphaned person from those bands, plus compensation for property destroyed. The Senate struck Chivington's name. Wikipedia reports the United States abrogated the treaty within two years and ignored its major provisions; the Medicine Lodge treaty (1867) cut reservation lands by about 90 percent.
land_lost_description: Treaty territory in Colorado (Fort Wise), lives (Sand Creek), and promised reparation lands.
acreage_if_known: Reparation grants promised: 4 x 320 acres + 160 acres per eligible person (treaty text)
legal_aftermath: Reparations: no verified payment in sources read (status [unverified]). Sand Creek Massacre National Historic Site dedicated Apr. 28, 2007; Colorado Gov. Hickenlooper apologized Dec. 3, 2014; about 3,478 acres added to the site in Oct. 2022 for tribal protection (per Wikipedia).

treaty_name: Treaty with the Kiowa and Comanche (Medicine Lodge), 15 Stat. 581
nations: Kiowa, Comanche, Plains Apache (Kiowa-Comanche-Apache Reservation)
mechanism_summary: Medicine Lodge (1867) and Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock (1903): allotment without the promised three-fourths consent -- Article 12 of the 1867 treaty (concluded Oct. 21, 1867; ratified July 25, 1868; proclaimed Aug. 25, 1868) said no cession of reservation land was valid unless signed by at least three-fourths of all adult male Indians occupying it. An 1892 allotment-and-cession agreement fell short of that threshold, was alleged fraudulent, and was altered by Congress; the Act of June 6, 1900 gave it effect. In Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock (Jan. 5, 1903) the Court held Congress has plenary authority over tribal relations, that this power is political and not subject to judicial control, that Congress may abrogate treaty provisions, and that courts cannot inquire into its motives.
land_lost_description: Reservation land allotted and 'surplus' opened to settlement.
acreage_if_known: about 2 million acres opened in 1901 [from-memory; not in sources read]
legal_aftermath: Lone Wolf is the foundational plenary-power case, still cited. Its presumption of congressional good faith was held inapplicable where Congress takes recognized-title property and must pay just compensation (Sioux Nation, 1980).
related_cases: Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock, 187 U.S. 553 (1903); United States v. Sioux Nation of Indians, 448 U.S. 371 (1980)

treaty_name: Medicine Lodge Treaty (1867) and 1869 executive order reservation
nations: Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes
mechanism_summary: Fort Reno: military reserve carved from the Cheyenne and Arapaho reservation (1883-2026) -- After the Medicine Lodge treaty, President Grant created the Cheyenne and Arapaho reservation by executive order (1869). About fourteen years later President Arthur set aside 9,493 acres as the Fort Reno military reservation. In 1948 the land passed to USDA. The tribes say they were never compensated for Fort Reno; federal officials argue prior settlements (a 1965 $15 million settlement based on an 1891 cession) resolved it. A 1949 bill returning about 6,900 acres passed the House in 1952 and stalled in the Senate. In 2026 a House farm bill draft (H.R. 7567) would make permanent a 2008 bar on USDA declaring the El Reno research facility excess; the House Agriculture Committee approved it 34-17 in early March 2026.
land_lost_description: About 6,700 acres west of Oklahoma City still held by USDA.
acreage_if_known: about 6,700 acres disputed (tribal accounting points to a discrepancy of about 10,000 acres)
legal_aftermath: Return still sought. Status of the farm-bill provision after committee approval was not verified (March 2026 source).

treaty_name: Treaty with the Sioux ... and Arapaho (Fort Laramie), 15 Stat. 635
nations: Lakota (Oglala, Sicangu/Brule, Minneconjou, Hunkpapa, Blackfeet, Sans Arc, Two Kettle), Yanktonai, Santee, and Arapaho; Oceti Sakowin
mechanism_summary: Fort Laramie 1868 and the Black Hills: abrogation by the Act of Feb. 28, 1877 -- Concluded April 29, 1868 (ratified Feb. 16, 1869; proclaimed Feb. 24, 1869). Article 2 set aside the Great Sioux Reservation, including the Black Hills, for 'absolute and undisturbed use and occupation.' Article 12 made any cession of reservation land invalid unless signed by at least three-fourths of all adult male Indians. Article 16 created 'unceded Indian territory' north of the North Platte and east of the Big Horn Mountains. Custer's 1874 expedition and the resulting gold rush brought thousands of non-Indians into the Hills, which the Army did not stop. In 1876 a commission obtained signatures from only about 10% of adult males; Congress enacted that 'agreement' as the Act of Feb. 28, 1877 (19 Stat. 254), which abrogated Article 16, took the Black Hills and the unceded territory, and substituted rations for the Hills and off-reservation hunting rights. In the Court's words, the 1877 Act was a taking of tribal property requiring just compensation.
land_lost_description: The Black Hills (Paha Sapa) and the unceded Powder River country; later the lands west of the Missouri redrawn in 1889 (V025).
acreage_if_known: Unceded territory about 33,000,000 acres from 1851 plus about 25,000,000 added (per a secondary summary of Art. 16)
legal_aftermath: 1923 suit under a jurisdictional act; Court of Claims dismissed 1942; Indian Claims Commission (1974, 4-1) held a taking; Court of Claims barred by res judicata 1975; Congress waived the bar 1978; Court of Claims affirmed 1979; Supreme Court (June 30, 1980) affirmed: $17.1 million principal (1877 value) plus 5% interest from 1877, about $105 million then. The award was never accepted. Fund reported over $1 billion by 2011 and about $2 billion by 2022 (journalistic figures; exact current balance not verified). The Lakota position is that the land was never for sale. In June 2026 resolutions from nine South Dakota tribes urged Congress to return federal public lands in the Black Hills. Pe' Sla: a 2026 exploratory drilling permit (Pete Lien & Sons; permit Feb. 27) near Pe' Sla was met by suits, a temporary restraining order, a week-long occupation (Apr. 30) and company withdrawal on about May 8, 2026.
related_cases: United States v. Sioux Nation of Indians, 448 U.S. 371 (1980); Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock, 187 U.S. 553 (1903) (distinguished)

treaty_name: Treaty of Fort Laramie (1868), Art. 12
nations: Lakota and Dakota bands of the Great Sioux Reservation
mechanism_summary: Act of March 2, 1889: the Great Sioux Reservation divided and about 9 million acres opened -- The Act of Mar. 2, 1889 (25 Stat. 888) divided the remaining Great Sioux Reservation into five smaller reservations (Standing Rock, Cheyenne River, Lower Brule, Rosebud, Pine Ridge), released Indian title to land outside them (Sec. 16), returned the remainder to the public domain for settlers at $1.25, $0.75 and $0.50 per acre (Sec. 21), and made the Act effective only upon acceptance and consent by the Sioux bands 'as prescribed by the twelfth article' of the 1868 treaty (Sec. 28). Whether the Article 12 three-fourths threshold was genuinely met is contested in the historical record; not resolved in sources read.
land_lost_description: About half of what remained of the Great Sioux Reservation.
legal_aftermath: The Sioux Nation case (1980) addressed the 1877 taking, not the 1889 cession. Diminishment of individual reservations was later litigated (V031, V033).
related_cases: Rosebud Sioux Tribe v. Kneip, 430 U.S. 584 (1977); Solem v. Bartlett, 465 U.S. 463 (1984)

treaty_name: Treaties of Traverse des Sioux and Mendota
nations: Dakota (Mdewakanton, Wahpekute, Sisseton, Wahpeton)
mechanism_summary: Dakota 1851 treaties, 1862 war and the Act of Feb. 16, 1863 -- The 1851 treaties (Traverse des Sioux, July 23; Mendota, Aug. 5) ceded large tracts of Minnesota Territory; the Senate struck the article that defined the reservation. Annuities were about two months late in summer 1862 and much compensation went to traders for disputed debts. The war began Aug. 18, 1862. Military commissions sentenced 303 men to death; Lincoln approved 38; they were hanged at Mankato on Dec. 26, 1862, the largest one-day mass execution in U.S. history. About 1,658 non-combatants were held at Fort Snelling, where an estimated 102 to 300 died. The Act of Feb. 16, 1863 (12 Stat. 652) declared the Dakota treaties annulled 'so far as said treaties or any of them purport to impose any future obligation on the United States' and forfeited all annuities to the United States. The Dakota were expelled from Minnesota; about 1,300 survivors were moved to Crow Creek in May 1863 and more than 200 died within six months; others went to the Santee Sioux Reservation in Nebraska. Minnesota offered a $25 scalp bounty.
land_lost_description: The Minnesota reservations and annuity entitlements; removal from the state.
legal_aftermath: Treaty obligations annulled by statute without individual findings of guilt (the Act applied to bands including non-participants; the details of individual exemptions, e.g., 208 Mdewakanton, are noted in secondary sources). Later land bases for survivors included Crow Creek and the Santee reservation in Nebraska.

treaty_name: Treaty with the Ponca, 12 Stat. 997
nations: Ponca (Ponca Tribe of Nebraska; Ponca Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma)
mechanism_summary: Ponca: 1858 treaty, the 1868 land error, 1877 removal and Standing Bear v. Crook (1879) -- The Ponca ceded land in the Mar. 12, 1858 treaty but kept a tract along the Niobrara and Ponca rivers, with the U.S. promising to protect them in possession 'during good behavior.' Through an error, the 1868 Fort Laramie treaty with the Sioux placed the Ponca reservation inside the Great Sioux Reservation (Wikipedia's Standing Bear article attributes the transfer to the Santee Dakota; sources vary). The Ponca were forced to Indian Territory in 1877; by spring 1878 nearly a third of the tribe had died of starvation and disease, including Standing Bear's son Bear Shield. Standing Bear and others walked home; the habeas corpus case United States ex rel. Standing Bear v. Crook was decided May 12, 1879 by Judge Elmer S. Dundy (D. Neb.), who held that 'an Indian is a person' within the meaning of habeas corpus and that the government had no legal basis to hold the Ponca. The Hayes administration allowed Standing Bear's group to return; an 1881 act returned about 26,236 acres in Knox County, Nebraska, and about half the tribe moved north.
land_lost_description: The Niobrara reservation (temporarily); about a third of the tribe in 1877-78.
legal_aftermath: Standing Bear v. Crook is a landmark on personhood, not a land judgment. The Northern Ponca were later terminated (effective 1966 per Wikipedia; the termination act itself believed 1962 [from-memory]) and restored as the Ponca Tribe of Nebraska on Oct. 31, 1990.
related_cases: United States ex rel. Standing Bear v. Crook, 25 F. Cas. 695 (C.C.D. Neb. 1879) [reporter citation from memory; not confirmed this session]

treaty_name: Treaty of Fort Laramie (1851); Fort Berthold agreements (1866 and later)
nations: Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara (MHA Nation / Three Affiliated Tribes)
mechanism_summary: Garrison Dam (1946-1956): the Fort Berthold Reservation and the Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara -- The Flood Control Act of 1944 (Pub. L. 78-534, Dec. 22, 1944) authorized the Missouri River Basin program including Garrison Dam. Despite repeated tribal refusals to sell, Public Law 437 (1949, the 'Taking Act') provided for acquisition of about 155,000 acres of Fort Berthold land; tribal leaders cited the 1851 treaty and a 1945 tribal resolution declaring the land their 'inherent property from time immemorial.' About 349 families were relocated. The gates closed in June 1953; the Lake Sakakawea reservoir was completed in 1956 and covers about 263.8 sq mi, about one-sixth of the reservation's surface. One source states the tribes lost roughly 95% of their land (reservation 9 million acres in 1851 to about 600,000 before the dam, per the 1949 tribal chairman), the highest share among Missouri River tribes.
land_lost_description: Most of the tribes' bottomland, towns and agricultural base.
legal_aftermath: The 1992 Equitable Compensation Act (Pub. L. 102-575) created a trust fund of $149.2 million for Fort Berthold (and $90.6 million for Standing Rock). MHA Nation's own accounts should be foregrounded.

treaty_name: Treaty of Fort Laramie (1868) and Great Sioux Reservation
nations: Standing Rock Sioux, Cheyenne River Sioux, Lower Brule Sioux, Crow Creek Sioux
mechanism_summary: Oahe Dam and Pick-Sloan: Standing Rock, Cheyenne River, Lower Brule and Crow Creek -- Under the Pick-Sloan program, Oahe Dam flooded more than 200,000 acres on the Standing Rock and Cheyenne River reservations (Wikipedia). For the Cheyenne River Sioux Tribe alone, Senate Report 106-217 states 104,492 acres of tribal land were acquired, four communities were flooded, 181 families (about 30% of the tribal population) were relocated and about 90% of the tribe's timber was lost. In 1954 the tribe asked for about $23.5 million; Congress authorized $10.6 million, and the report states non-Indian owners received $49.22 per acre against $21.49 for the tribe.
land_lost_description: Riverbottom forests, towns, agricultural land and the Missouri riparian corridor.
acreage_if_known: 104,492 acres (Cheyenne River Sioux Tribe); more than 200,000 acres across Standing Rock and Cheyenne River per Wikipedia
legal_aftermath: Later equitable compensation trust funds: Standing Rock $90.6M (Pub. L. 102-575, 1992); Fort Berthold $149.2M (same act); Crow Creek $27.5M (Pub. L. 104-223, 1996); Lower Brule $39.3M (Pub. L. 105-132, 1997); Cheyenne River bill S. 964 recommended in 1999 with $290.7M principal (enactment not confirmed in sources read).

treaty_name: Treaties of Fort Laramie (1851, 1868) invoked by the Tribe
nations: Standing Rock Sioux Tribe (and allied Oceti Sakowin nations)
mechanism_summary: Dakota Access Pipeline and Lake Oahe (2016-2026): context, not an adjudicated treaty violation -- The Army Corps approved easements for the Lake Oahe crossing on July 26, 2016; construction near Oahe was halted Sept. 9 and the easement denied Dec. 4, 2016; a Jan. 24, 2017 presidential memorandum led to approval Feb. 8, 2017. Courts decided the matter on NEPA grounds: D.D.C. ordered a full EIS (Mar. 25, 2020) and vacated the easement (July 6, 2020); the D.C. Circuit affirmed that the Corps violated NEPA but reversed the shutdown order (Jan. 26, 2021); certiorari denied Feb. 22, 2022. The Corps issued a final EIS Dec. 19, 2025 and a Record of Decision May 21, 2026 selecting Alternative 4 (easement with added conditions). The Tribe voluntarily dismissed a related challenge; dismissal June 23, 2026. Treaty-based claims were part of the Tribe's public case, but the controlling rulings summarized in the tracker concern NEPA.
land_lost_description: (No land taking; the dispute is about the pipeline crossing near the reservation, the 1958 Oahe taking context, and consultation.)
legal_aftermath: Pipeline operating; easement authorized in 2026 on conditions. Include in the atlas as 'modern conflict', not as a catalogued treaty breach.
related_cases: Standing Rock Sioux Tribe v. U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (D.D.C./D.C. Cir.) [docket numbers not confirmed this session]

treaty_name: Treaty of Fort Laramie (1868); Act of 1889
nations: Rosebud Sioux Tribe (Sicangu Lakota)
mechanism_summary: Rosebud Sioux Tribe v. Kneip (1977): the 1904 Act diminishes the Rosebud Reservation -- Congress ratified a 1901 agreement and passed acts in 1904, 1907 and 1910 ceding and opening unallotted lands in Gregory, Tripp, Lyman and Mellette counties. The Supreme Court (Apr. 4, 1977, Rehnquist) held the 1904 Act 'clearly evidence[d] a congressional intent to diminish the boundaries' for Gregory County and that the 1907 and 1910 Acts continued that intent, even though the three-fourths tribal consent was not obtained and payment shifted from a lump sum. Marshall, Brennan and Stewart dissented.
land_lost_description: Reservation boundaries (jurisdiction) in the opened counties.
legal_aftermath: Boundaries diminished as a matter of federal law (jurisdiction); the Tribe continues to hold trust land within the opened area.
related_cases: Rosebud Sioux Tribe v. Kneip, 430 U.S. 584 (1977)

treaty_name: Treaty with the Sisseton and Wahpeton Sioux (1867); Agreement of 1889
nations: Sisseton-Wahpeton Oyate (Dakota)
mechanism_summary: Lake Traverse Reservation (Sisseton-Wahpeton) and DeCoteau v. District County Court (1975) -- Under an 1889 agreement the Tribe ceded all unallotted lands within the 1867 reservation boundaries to the United States for a sum certain; the Act of Mar. 3, 1891 implemented it. In DeCoteau (Mar. 3, 1975, 6-3) the Court held the 1891 Act 'terminated' the Lake Traverse Reservation, so South Dakota courts have civil and criminal jurisdiction over tribal members on non-Indian, unallotted lands within the old boundaries.
land_lost_description: Reservation status over ceded and opened lands.
legal_aftermath: Jurisdictional disestablishment affirmed by Supreme Court; contrasts with Solem/McGirt where Congress's cession language was absent.
related_cases: DeCoteau v. District County Court, 420 U.S. 425 (1975)

treaty_name: Treaty of Fort Laramie (1868); Omaha treaties
nations: Cheyenne River Sioux; Omaha Tribe of Nebraska
mechanism_summary: Claims that failed: Cheyenne River (Solem v. Bartlett, 1984) and Omaha (Nebraska v. Parker, 2016) were not diminished -- Surplus-land acts do not automatically shrink a reservation. In Solem (Feb. 22, 1984, unanimous), the Cheyenne River Act of 1908 authorized the Secretary to 'sell and dispose' of about 1.6 million acres for homesteading with proceeds credited to the Tribe; the Court read the Secretary as the Tribe's sales agent, not as a cession, and applied a framework weighing (1) statutory language, (2) circumstances of passage and (3) subsequent events. In Nebraska v. Parker (Mar. 22, 2016, unanimous, Thomas) the 1882 Act 'merely opened reservation land to settlement' and did not diminish the Omaha Reservation; later demographics and settler expectations could not override the text.
land_lost_description: (Reservation boundaries survived.)
acreage_if_known: Solem: about 1.6 million acres opened but still reservation
legal_aftermath: These cases, with McGirt (V047), define the modern rule: only Congress can diminish, and intent must be clear.
related_cases: Solem v. Bartlett, 465 U.S. 463 (1984); Nebraska v. Parker, 577 U.S. 481 (2016)

treaty_name: Crow Treaty of 1868 (15 Stat. 649)
nations: Crow Tribe (Apsaalooke)
mechanism_summary: Crow Tribe and Herrera v. Wyoming (2019): treaty hunting right survives statehood -- The 1868 treaty reserved the right to hunt on 'unoccupied lands of the United States' so long as game may be found. Wyoming prosecuted a tribal member for elk hunting in the Bighorn National Forest, arguing the right expired at statehood and that the forest was 'occupied.' The Supreme Court (May 20, 2019, 5-4, Sotomayor) held the right survived the Wyoming Statehood Act and that Bighorn National Forest was not categorically 'occupied'; it left open whether particular areas were occupied and whether Wyoming could regulate for conservation.
land_lost_description: (Rights upheld; state prosecution reversed.)
legal_aftermath: Counterexample in the hunting/fishing line (Winans 1905, Fishing Vessel 1979, Mille Lacs 1999, Cougar Den 2019).
related_cases: Herrera v. Wyoming, 587 U.S. ___ (2019); Ward v. Race Horse, 163 U.S. 504 (1896) [from-memory, overruled in effect by Mille Lacs]

treaty_name: Treaty of Ruby Valley, 18 Stat. 689
nations: Western Shoshone (Newe)
mechanism_summary: Western Shoshone: Treaty of Ruby Valley (1863) and the ICC payment the Nation refuses -- Signed Oct. 1, 1863 by Governors Nye and Doty and twelve chiefs, the treaty (18 Stat. 689-692) granted access, passage and resource rights; it did not cede land. A 1951 claim (ICC Docket 326-K) alleged loss of aboriginal title; the Commission treated the land as extinguished by encroachment and awarded money; Congress appropriated $26 million for 24 million acres in 1979. Tribes refused the payment. In United States v. Dann (Feb. 20, 1985, unanimous) the Court held 'payment' under the ICC Act occurred when funds were placed in a Treasury trust account for the Tribe, so the claim was final; it did not decide whether title was actually extinguished. A Western Shoshone National Council quiet-title suit was dismissed Jan. 17, 2006. On Mar. 10, 2006 the U.N. Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination cited credible information that Western Shoshone land rights were being denied.
land_lost_description: Aboriginal-title claim to about 24-26 million acres (the treaty territory is about 40,000 sq mi per Wikipedia).
acreage_if_known: about 24 million acres (ICC award basis); about 40,000 sq mi claimed territory
legal_aftermath: The payment fund remains unaccepted by many; a 2004 distribution act was opposed by seven of nine tribal councils (figures vary between $145M and $160M in sources).
related_cases: United States v. Dann, 470 U.S. 39 (1985); United States v. Western Shoshone National Council, 415 F. Supp. 2d 1201 (D. Nev. 2006) [from Wikipedia]

treaty_name: Treaty of Box Elder (Treaty with the Northwestern Bands of Shoshone)
nations: Northwestern Bands of Shoshone
mechanism_summary: Box Elder (Fort Bridger) 1863: no recognized title, no compensation (Northwestern Shoshone) -- The July 30, 1863 treaty promised peace, travel routes and increased annuities, and Article IV described the 'country claimed' by Chief Pokatello. The Senate later added an amendment saying the treaty admitted no greater title than existed under Mexican law. When the Bands sought about $15 million for roughly 15 million acres under a 1929 jurisdictional act, the Supreme Court (Mar. 12, 1945) held the treaty did not recognize or acknowledge Indian title, so the claim did not arise under the treaty; they recovered nothing. Roberts, Douglas, Frankfurter and Murphy dissented.
land_lost_description: Claim to about 15 million acres.
legal_aftermath: No recovery under this case; later ICC claims for Shoshone bands exist but were not verified. Sets the pre-Tee-Hit-Ton pattern: no recognition by Congress, no compensation.
related_cases: Northwestern Bands of Shoshone Indians v. United States, 324 U.S. 335 (1945); Tee-Hit-Ton Indians v. United States, 348 U.S. 272 (1955)

treaty_name: Lame Bull Treaty (1855); 1895 Agreement ceding mountain land
nations: Blackfeet (Pikuni) Nation
mechanism_summary: Blackfeet and Glacier National Park: the 1895 agreement and the 1910 park -- The Lame Bull Treaty (1855) included the eastern part of today's park within the Blackfeet reservation up to the Continental Divide. Under an 1895 agreement, Chief White Calf authorized sale of about 800,000 acres of mountain land to the United States for $1.5 million; the Blackfeet understood they would keep hunting rights as long as the land remained 'public land of the United States.' Glacier became a national park on May 11, 1910; the enabling legislation does not mention the guarantees. The United States holds the park designation ended those rights, which the Court of Claims confirmed in 1935. Park rules prohibit hunting; some Blackfeet maintain the usage rights persist.
land_lost_description: About 800,000 acres of mountain land and associated hunting/gathering access.
legal_aftermath: Court of Claims (1935) sided with the United States; Blackfeet claims that rights persist de jure remain.
related_cases: Court of Claims (1935) decision [citation not confirmed]

treaty_name: Treaty with the Nez Perce (1855), 12 Stat. 957; Treaty with the Nez Perces (1863), 14 Stat. 647
nations: Nez Perce (Nimiipuu), including the Wallowa and other non-treaty bands
mechanism_summary: Nez Perce: the 1855 reservation, the 1863 'thief treaty,' and 1877 -- The 1855 treaty (June 11, 1855; ratified Mar. 8, 1859) set a large reservation (about 7.5 million acres per a secondary source). The June 9, 1863 treaty (ratified Apr. 17, 1867; 14 Stat. 647) was signed at Lapwai by about 51 chiefs, headmen and delegates [unverified: V2 found no signer count for the 1863 treaty; the 1855 treaty OCR shows about 58 Nez Perce signers, so the count may be from the wrong treaty] with Lawyer as head chief, and reduced the reservation by about 90% to roughly 750,000 acres. Many Nez Perce, including Chief Joseph's Wallowa band in northeastern Oregon, rejected it: the bands whose homelands were ceded had not agreed. The name 'thief treaty' is used in the literature [from-memory] for a treaty signed by a faction. In May 1877 Gen. O. O. Howard gave the non-treaty bands 30 days to move; the Nez Perce War ran June 14-Oct. 5, 1877 (a fighting retreat of about 1,170 miles). After the surrender at Bear Paw, 418 surrendered and 150-200 escaped to Canada; prisoners were sent to Fort Leavenworth and Indian Territory; 268 survivors returned to the Northwest in 1885, and Joseph was not allowed to return to Idaho.
land_lost_description: About 90% of the 1855 reservation; the Wallowa homeland.
legal_aftermath: No general restoration; the Nez Perce Tribe of Idaho and the Colville Confederated Tribes hold the history. Specific later land recoveries (Wallowa) not verified.

treaty_name: Treaty with the Ute (1868), 15 Stat. 619; Brunot Agreement (1873-74); Act of June 15, 1880, 21 Stat. 199
nations: Ute (Northern Ute/Uintah and Ouray, Ute Mountain Ute, Southern Ute)
mechanism_summary: Ute: the 1868 Colorado reservation, Brunot (1873), the 1880 Act, 1881 removal, and Hagen v. Utah (1994) -- The treaty of Mar. 2, 1868 (proclaimed Nov. 6, 1868) set aside the western portion of Colorado for the Ute's 'absolute and undisturbed use and occupation.' After silver was found in the San Juan Mountains (1872), the Brunot Agreement (ratified 1873) gave the United States the mineral-rich land. After the 1879 White River (Meeker) conflict, the Act of June 15, 1880 (ch. 223) accepted an agreement with the confederated Ute bands to sell their Colorado reservation and settle members in severalty, withheld the White River Utes' share until the 'guilty parties' were surrendered, and required consent of three-fourths of adult males. In 1881 the Uncompahgre and White River Ute were forced west to reservations in Utah. In Hagen v. Utah (Feb. 23, 1994) the Court held Congress diminished the Uintah Valley Reservation when it opened unallotted lands, so Myton is not Indian country.
land_lost_description: Nearly all of the western Colorado reservation; Uintah Valley reservation diminished.
acreage_if_known: San Juan cession about 3.7 million acres [from-memory]
legal_aftermath: Hagen (1994) treated the opened Uintah lands as no longer reservation for jurisdiction. Subsequent Ute/Utah jurisdiction litigation not verified this session. In 2026 press reports describe Utah legislative moves complicating Ute land-return hopes (headline only).
related_cases: Hagen v. Utah, 510 U.S. 399 (1994)

treaty_name: Treaty with the Navaho, 15 Stat. 667
nations: Navajo Nation (Dine) and Mescalero Apache
mechanism_summary: Navajo: the Long Walk and Bosque Redondo (1864-1868), ended by the 1868 treaty -- Beginning in early 1864 the Army forced the Navajo to Fort Sumner (Bosque Redondo), New Mexico; more than 300 died on the Long Walk (one source), and over 9,000 Navajo and Mescalero were interned there, about 8,500 Navajo and 500 Mescalero in April 1865 against a plan for 5,000. Bosque Redondo was not a violation of a ratified treaty in force; it was a coerced removal and confinement during war. The June 1, 1868 treaty (ratified July 25; proclaimed Aug. 12) ended the war, set apart a reservation for the Navajo's 'use and occupation' and let them return after it was signed (treaty dated June 1, 1868; the return march is commonly dated June 18, 1868, not verified this session). 'May 1868' predates the treaty and appears to be an error propagated from Wikipedia. Article 13 made the reservation their 'permanent home.' The reservation later grew to about 17.5 million acres (17,544,500 acres per Wikipedia, Navajo Nation).
land_lost_description: Four years of confinement, deaths, and homeland access.
acreage_if_known: Return to homeland; later reservation about 17.5 million acres (17,544,500 acres per Wikipedia, Navajo Nation)
legal_aftermath: The 1868 treaty is the rare case where a treaty restored people to their homeland. Modern shortfalls concern water (V041).

treaty_name: Treaty with the Navaho, 15 Stat. 667
nations: Navajo Nation
mechanism_summary: Navajo water: the 1868 treaty reserves water but creates no duty to secure it (Arizona v. Navajo Nation, 2023) -- The Navajo Nation asked the courts to order the United States to assess its water needs and develop a plan to secure Colorado River water. The Supreme Court (June 22, 2023, 5-4, Kavanaugh; Gorsuch, Sotomayor, Kagan and Jackson dissenting) held that the 1868 treaty reserved the water needed to serve the reservation's purpose, but did not require the United States to take affirmative steps to secure it, stating 'Indian treaties cannot be rewritten or expanded beyond their clear terms.' The baseline doctrine is Winters v. United States (1908): the 1888 agreement creating Fort Belknap impliedly reserved enough Milk River water, statehood did not cancel it, and ambiguities are resolved from the Indians' standpoint.
land_lost_description: Unquantified Colorado River water rights.
legal_aftermath: Right acknowledged in principle; duty to secure denied. Negotiated settlements remain the route.
related_cases: Arizona v. Navajo Nation, 599 U.S. ___ (2023); Winters v. United States, 207 U.S. 564 (1908)

treaty_name: Cochise-Howard agreement (1872), executive order reservation; Treaty of Santa Fe (1852) with the Apache
nations: Chiricahua Apache (Ndee/Ndé); Fort Sill Apache Tribe; Mescalero Apache Tribe
mechanism_summary: Chiricahua Apache: the 1872 reservation abolished (1876) and 27 years as prisoners of war (1886-1912/14) -- Gen. Oliver O. Howard, with Thomas Jeffords, negotiated peace with Cochise; an executive order of Dec. 14, 1872 created the Chiricahua Reservation in southeastern Arizona. This was an executive-order reservation based on an informal agreement, not a ratified treaty. In 1876 it was restored to the public domain and the Chiricahua and other bands were moved to San Carlos. After Geronimo, Naiche and 34 holdouts surrendered in September 1886, most remaining Chiricahua, including Army scouts who had served the U.S., were exiled as prisoners to Fort Marion, Florida, then Alabama, then Fort Sill, Oklahoma. Congress released the prisoners in August 1912 (per Wikipedia); 183 people (about two-thirds) moved to the Mescalero reservation and 78 stayed in Oklahoma. Other sources place the relocation in 1913-14.
land_lost_description: The Chiricahua homeland reservation; family separation; 26-28 years of captivity.
legal_aftermath: No land return; the Fort Sill Apache Tribe in Oklahoma and Mescalero Apache Tribe in New Mexico are the descendant governments.

treaty_name: Seminole treaties (1856, 1866); Curtis Act sec. 19
nations: Seminole Nation of Oklahoma
mechanism_summary: Seminole Nation v. United States (1942): annuities paid to corrupt officials despite treaty duties -- The Nation sued for treaty payments allegedly misdirected to tribal officers who defrauded members, with U.S. officials knowing. The Supreme Court (May 11, 1942, Murphy) held the Government owes Indian tribes a fiduciary duty judged by 'strict standards'; payments made at a council's request do not discharge the obligation if officials knew the council was defrauding members; it remanded for findings on 1870-74 and 1899-1907. This is the doctrinal root of the trust-based breach claim, later used to cabin the Indian Claims Commission and Tucker Act litigation.
land_lost_description: Money (annuities), not land.
legal_aftermath: Remanded for findings; the case is the leading authority on payment to fiduciaries and government knowledge.
related_cases: Seminole Nation v. United States, 316 U.S. 286 (1942); United States v. Dann, 470 U.S. 39 (1985) (applies Seminole common-law payment rule)

treaty_name: Treaties of 1830s removal; 1866 reconstruction treaties
nations: Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Muscogee (Creek), Seminole (the Five Tribes)
mechanism_summary: Curtis Act (1898) and Oklahoma statehood (1907): Five Tribes governments dismantled and lands allotted -- The Curtis Act (1898) extended allotment to the Five Tribes, ended their self-government and tribal courts, and provided for sale of 'surplus' lands. Oklahoma statehood followed in 1907. This overrode treaty guarantees such as the Creeks' 1856 promise of no annexation to a State and the 1866 promise that remaining land be 'forever set apart.' Congress did not use language of cession or disestablishment for the Creek (McGirt), but practice under Curtis erased tribal government and moved most land out of Indian hands for decades.
land_lost_description: Tribal governments (until reorganization) and most communal land.
legal_aftermath: Reservations were held never disestablished in McGirt (2020), V047.
related_cases: McGirt v. Oklahoma, 591 U.S. ___ (2020)

treaty_name: Many treaties with communal-title reservations (e.g., Fort Laramie 1868, Medicine Lodge 1867)
nations: Most reservation tribes outside the Five Tribes at first; extended to the Five Tribes by the Curtis Act (1898)
mechanism_summary: The General Allotment (Dawes) Act of 1887 and the loss of the communal land base -- The Act of Feb. 8, 1887 (24 Stat. 388) authorized allotment of reservation land in severalty: 160 acres to a head of family, 80 acres to a single person over 18 or an orphan, 40 acres to other single persons under 18. Allotments were held in trust for 25 years (Sec. 5). After allotments were made, the Secretary could negotiate with the tribe to buy 'surplus' reservation land, with Congress to ratify; the land was reserved for actual settlers, limited to 160 acres per person. Later statutes (Burke Act 1906, which allowed fee patents to 'competent' allottees, and individual 'surplus land' acts) accelerated land loss. The Indian Reorganization Act (1934) ended further allotment. A common summary: Indian-held land fell from about 138 million acres (1887) to about 48 million acres (1934). Fractionated heirship later left about 4 million owner interests in about 10 million acres of trust allotments (2004 House figures).
land_lost_description: About 90 million acres, roughly two-thirds of the 1887 base (secondary summary).
legal_aftermath: Federal courts treat allotment alone as insufficient to diminish a reservation (McGirt 2020; Solem 1984), but surplus-land acts with cession language can (Hagen 1994; Rosebud 1977; DeCoteau 1975). Land buy-back efforts (Cobell settlement, 2010s) and trust-land restoration continue; see B3.
related_cases: Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock, 187 U.S. 553 (1903); McGirt v. Oklahoma, 591 U.S. ___ (2020)

treaty_name: Treaties and trust relationships of the named tribes (e.g., Klamath 1864, Menominee 1854)
nations: More than 100 tribes and bands over the period (counts vary); named in HCR 108: Flathead, Klamath, Menominee, Potawatomi (KS/NE), Turtle Mountain Chippewa, and all tribes in California, Florida, New York and Texas
mechanism_summary: Termination policy: House Concurrent Resolution 108 (1953) and Public Law 280 -- HCR 108 (Aug. 1, 1953) declared the sense of Congress that Indians should be 'freed from Federal supervision and control and from all disabilities and limitations specially applicable to Indians,' and named the tribes above. Public Law 280 (Aug. 15, 1953, 67 Stat. 588) gave California, Minnesota (except Red Lake), Nebraska, Oregon (except Warm Springs) and Wisconsin (except Menominee) criminal and civil jurisdiction in Indian country and let other states assume it. Its codification (18 U.S.C. 1162(b)) preserves hunting, trapping and fishing rights secured by federal treaty, agreement or statute. The National Archives states that Congress began 60 separate termination proceedings between 1953 and 1970, and that over three million acres of tribal land were relinquished; the Nixon administration repudiated termination in 1970.
land_lost_description: Federal recognition and trust status; reservation land; treaty-based services.
legal_aftermath: Many terminated tribes were restored by statute from 1973 on (Menominee 1973, Siletz 1977, Klamath 1986, Ponca 1990, Catawba 1993). Menominee Tribe v. United States (1968) read PL 280 with the Termination Act to preserve treaty hunting and fishing rights.
related_cases: Menominee Tribe v. United States, 391 U.S. 404 (1968)

nations: Muscogee (Creek) Nation; by extension the Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw and Seminole Nations
mechanism_summary: McGirt v. Oklahoma (2020): the Muscogee (Creek) Reservation was never disestablished -- Oklahoma had long exercised criminal jurisdiction over most of eastern Oklahoma on the premise that allotment and statehood ended the Creek reservation. In McGirt (July 9, 2020, 5-4, Gorsuch) the Court held that, for purposes of the Major Crimes Act, land reserved for the Creek Nation in the 19th century remains Indian country: only Congress can disestablish a reservation, it must clearly express that intent (typically explicit cession or total-surrender language), and no allotment-era statute did so. Allotment alone is 'a first step rather than a final one.' Extratextual evidence (demographics, historical practice) cannot override text. The Court said Congress remains free to change the framework. Aftermath: the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals ruled in Sept. 2021 that McGirt is not retroactive; the Court declined challenges in Feb. 2022. The Cherokee Nation refiled over 500 dismissed cases. Roughly 1,900 prisoners were affected, about 10% qualifying for rehearings (Wikipedia).
land_lost_description: (Reversal of presumed loss: jurisdiction recognized.)
acreage_if_known: The Creek reservation area (about 3 million acres by the 1866 cession terms is [from-memory])
legal_aftermath: Judicially recognized: Muscogee (Creek) Reservation intact for MCA purposes; extended in practice to the other four tribes' reservations by Oklahoma appellate courts. Castro-Huerta (2022) then expanded state jurisdiction over non-Indian offenders (V048).
related_cases: McGirt v. Oklahoma, 591 U.S. ___ (2020); Sharp v. Murphy (2020); Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta, 597 U.S. ___ (2022)

treaty_name: Worcester v. Georgia line; treaties promising self-government and exclusion of state authority
nations: All tribes with Indian country in states; the case arose in the Cherokee Nation Reservation
mechanism_summary: Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta (2022): concurrent state jurisdiction over non-Indians in Indian country -- The Court held (June 29, 2022, 5-4, Kavanaugh) that the federal government and the State have concurrent jurisdiction to prosecute crimes by non-Indians against Indians in Indian country. The majority reasoned that the Worcester-era presumption that states lack jurisdiction had weakened and that the General Crimes Act, as codified in 1948, no longer treated tribal lands as distinct from state territory; state prosecution does not strip tribal authority because tribes cannot prosecute non-Indians. Gorsuch (joined by Breyer, Sotomayor, Kagan) dissented: 'Where this Court once stood firm, today it wilts.' This is a judicial reinterpretation of federal-state allocation, not a congressional abrogation; whether it 'violates' treaties is contested.
land_lost_description: Exclusivity of federal jurisdiction (and so tribal-federal relationship) over non-Indian offenders against Native victims.
legal_aftermath: Tribes and amici call for legislation; Gorsuch's dissent invites Congress to act. After the decision, FBI jurisdiction expanded, per one secondary account, to almost 45% of Oklahoma's land.
related_cases: Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta, 597 U.S. ___ (2022); Worcester v. Georgia, 31 U.S. (6 Pet.) 515 (1832)

treaty_name: Treaty of Santa Fe (1852) invoked by Apache Stronghold; Public Land Order 1229 (1955)
nations: San Carlos Apache, Tonto Apache and other Western Apache communities; Apache Stronghold (nonprofit)
mechanism_summary: Oak Flat (Chi'chil Bildagoteel): 2014 land exchange, Apache Stronghold litigation and the March 2026 transfer -- A 2014 provision added to a defense bill (Sen. John McCain) authorized swapping 2,422 acres of the Tonto National Forest, including Oak Flat, to Resolution Copper. The land had been shielded from mining for nearly 60 years under a 1955 Eisenhower order. The U.S. Supreme Court rejected Apache Stronghold's appeal in May 2025; on Mar. 13, 2026 the Ninth Circuit denied an injunction; the Forest Service transferred Oak Flat to Resolution Copper on Mar. 16, 2026. Opponents continue to litigate; estimates cited are a copper deposit worth about $150 billion and a crater more than 1,000 feet deep. The 1852 treaty argument and religious-freedom claims are the Apache Stronghold legal theories; courts have not accepted them (treaty theory status [from-memory]).
land_lost_description: Sacred and recreational lands; ceremonial access.
legal_aftermath: Transferred; litigation continuing as of March 2026. Needs updating after Oct. 2026 (NARF index lists further 9th Circuit and Supreme Court filings in Sept. 2026, headlines only).
related_cases: Apache Stronghold v. United States (9th Cir. en banc 2024) [from-memory]; cert. denied (May 2025) per Cronkite News

treaty_name: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848), Arts. VIII-IX (context)
nations: Taos Pueblo (Red Willow People)
mechanism_summary: Taos Pueblo and Blue Lake: taken in 1906, returned in 1970 -- About 48,000 acres of Taos Pueblo's sacred mountain watershed were taken in 1906 and included in what became the Carson National Forest (the Taos Pueblo website gives 1906; Wikipedia says 'early 20th century'). The Pueblo sought return of the land, not compensation. Congress returned it in Public Law 91-550 (84 Stat. 1437), approved Dec. 15, 1970: the land is 'held by the United States in trust for the Pueblo de Taos'; the statute recites that the Taos Indians depend on the lands for water, forage, wood and timber and for religious ceremonials. An additional 764 acres followed in 1996 (Wikipedia). It is widely regarded as the first major modern U.S. return of land to a tribe.
land_lost_description: 48,000 acres, 1906-1970; Blue Lake and watershed.
legal_aftermath: Land RETURNED (see B3). Whether the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo's property protections apply to Pueblo lands is a legal-history question not resolved here; list as context.

treaty_name: Treaty of Medicine Creek, 10 Stat. 1132
nations: Nisqually, Puyallup, Steilacoom, Squaxin Island and other Puget Sound bands
mechanism_summary: Treaty of Medicine Creek (1854): small reservations, the Nisqually War, Leschi, and the Puyallup claims -- Gov. Isaac Stevens and 62 leaders signed on Dec. 26, 1854 (ratified Mar. 3, 1855; proclaimed Apr. 10, 1855); the tribes ceded about 2.24 million acres for reservations of about two sections each (e.g., two 1,280-acre tracts plus Klah-che-min Island), $32,500 over 20 years (Art. 4 schedule runs 20 years; the itemized installments sum to $32,250, which is $250 below the stated total), and the Article 3 right of taking fish at 'all usual and accustomed grounds and stations' in common with citizens. Nisqually leader Leschi protested that the reservation was forested, rocky, unsuited to farming and had no access to the Nisqually River; he led resistance in the 1855-56 war, was arrested on a murder charge, hanged at Steilacoom on Feb. 19, 1858, and exonerated by a historical court in 2004. Reservations were enlarged in January 1857. The Puyallup lost most of their allotted reservation land through questionable transactions; the Puyallup Tribe of Indians Settlement Act of 1989 (Pub. L. 101-41) ratified a settlement worth about $162 million in total, including trust lands in the Tacoma tideflats (a few hundred acres, per the act's listing), a $22 million trust fund and $10 million for economic development and land, in return for the Tribe relinquishing claims to roughly 20,000 acres in the Tacoma area.
land_lost_description: About 2.24 million acres; riverine access; allotments.
acreage_if_known: 2.24 million acres ceded (Wikipedia, 'Treaty of Medicine Creek'); HistoryLink essay 21193 instead says about 3,960 square miles (about 2.53 million acres); the treaty text gives no acreage; Puyallup claim of more than 20,000 acres relinquished in 1989-90
legal_aftermath: Settlement (1989-90) rather than restoration. Fishing right litigated in V052.
related_cases: Puyallup Tribe v. Department of Game, 391 U.S. 392 (1968) (decided May 27, 1968) [verified]

treaty_name: Stevens Treaties (Medicine Creek, Point Elliott, Point No Point, Neah Bay, Quinault, Yakama)
nations: Treaty tribes of western Washington, including Nisqually, Puyallup, Lummi, Suquamish and others
mechanism_summary: Stevens treaty fishing rights: Boldt (1974) and Washington v. Fishing Vessel Ass'n (1979) -- The treaties secured 'the right of taking fish, at all usual and accustomed grounds and stations ... in common with all citizens of the Territory.' For decades Washington regulated and arrested treaty fishers. Judge George Boldt (W.D. Wash.) in United States v. Washington, 384 F. Supp. 312 (1974), read 'in common with' as equal sharing, giving treaty and non-treaty fishers each up to 50% of the harvestable fish; the formula gave tribes about 43% of the Puget Sound harvest (about 18% statewide). The Ninth Circuit affirmed in 1975. When the state would not enforce the order, Boldt directed the Coast Guard and National Marine Fisheries Service to do so. The Supreme Court (July 2, 1979, Stevens) largely upheld the ruling: the treaties guarantee a share of each run, an equitable division begins with roughly equal shares, and the 50% figure is a ceiling that can fall if tribal needs can be met with less. Tribal share of the harvest rose from under 5% before the ruling to 49% by 1984 (Wikipedia), and tribes became co-managers.
land_lost_description: (Decades of denied fishing access; later recovered.)
legal_aftermath: Rights confirmed and implemented; ongoing disputes include the culvert case (2007 ruling affirmed by the Ninth Circuit in 2016, per Wikipedia).
related_cases: United States v. Washington, 384 F. Supp. 312 (W.D. Wash. 1974); Washington v. Fishing Vessel Ass'n, 443 U.S. 658 (1979)

treaty_name: Treaty with the Yakama (June 9, 1855; proclaimed 1859), 12 Stat. 951
nations: Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakama Nation
mechanism_summary: Yakama treaty rights: Winans (1905) and Cougar Den (2019) -- In Winans (May 16, 1905) the Court held the Yakama fishing right at usual and accustomed places was 'a reservation by the Indians of rights already possessed and not granted away by them,' a continuing servitude binding the United States, its grantees, the State and its grantees; statehood did not defeat it. In Cougar Den (Mar. 19, 2019, 5-4, Breyer plurality) the 1855 treaty's right 'to travel upon all public highways' preempted Washington's fuel tax as applied to importing fuel for sale on the reservation. The Yakama Nation continues to contest state action burdening these rights.
land_lost_description: (Rights asserted and upheld.)
legal_aftermath: Upheld. Winans introduced the 'reserved rights' canon: treaties are a grant of rights from the Indians, not to them.
related_cases: United States v. Winans, 198 U.S. 371 (1905); Washington State Dep't of Licensing v. Cougar Den, Inc., 586 U.S. ___ (2019)

treaty_name: Eighteen treaties negotiated by Redick McKee, George W. Barbour and Oliver M. Wozencraft
nations: More than 100 California tribes and bands (Pomo, Miwok, Yokuts, Maidu, Wintun, Yurok and others)
mechanism_summary: California: 18 unratified treaties (1851-52) and the secrecy until 1905 -- Between Mar. 19, 1851 and Jan. 7, 1852 three federal commissioners negotiated 18 treaties reserving land for tribes. They were submitted to the Senate on June 1, 1852 and rejected in closed session (a citation dates the action July 8, 1852) after California's state government lobbied against them; Historian William Ellison suggests the large land reservations and costs made them unpopular. The treaties were sealed from the public until Jan. 18, 1905. The tribes had given up claims on the strength of promises that were never ratified. The reservations totaled about 11,700 square miles, roughly 7% of California (about 7.5 million acres). Historian Benjamin Madley estimates that at least 9,400 to 16,000 California Indians were killed by non-Indians between 1846 and 1873.
land_lost_description: Everything that was to be reserved, plus aboriginal lands ceded in the course of the negotiations.
acreage_if_known: about 7.5 million acres (about 7% of California; one Wikipedia page's 'one-seventh' is inconsistent)
legal_aftermath: Compensation came only through later claims: the often-cited 1964 Indian Claims Commission award of about $29 million at about 47 cents per acre [from-memory; not verified here]; a different Wikipedia passage lists $17.5 million (1944) and $46 million (1946). No land was returned.
related_cases: Indians of California v. United States, 98 Ct. Cl. 583 (1942) [from-memory]

treaty_name: Rogue River treaties (1853-55); Coast Reservation by executive order (1855)
nations: Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians; Western Oregon tribes
mechanism_summary: Siletz and Western Oregon: Coast Reservation reduced, tribes terminated (1954), restored (1977) -- An executive order of Nov. 9, 1855 created the Coast Indian Reservation (about 1.1 million acres), weeks into the final phase of the Rogue River Wars; most affected peoples were moved onto it. The reservation was reduced by roughly three-quarters (about 900,000 acres) in 1865 and 1875, which Wikipedia says violated treaties; a Siletz official said another 700,000 acres were removed in 1875. The Western Oregon Indian Termination Act (Pub. L. 588, Aug. 13, 1954) ended federal supervision; the remaining lands were sold except for Government Hill. The Siletz Restoration Act (Nov. 18, 1977) restored recognition and the Siletz Reservation Act (1980) returned about 3,660 acres. In 2026 the Tribe acquired about 6.82 acres at Rocky Shores near Yachats for $120,000 through partners (McKenzie River Trust, View the Future and The Nature Conservancy), with a tribal official saying 'those promises were broken.' (Closing was pending at the time of the source.)
land_lost_description: About 900,000 acres of the Coast Reservation plus termination-era losses.
legal_aftermath: Restoration 1977/1980; small purchases continue (2026).

treaty_name: Treaty with the Klamath, Modoc and Yahooskin Band of Snake Indians, 16 Stat. 707
nations: Klamath Tribes (Klamath, Modoc, Yahooskin Band of Snake)
mechanism_summary: Klamath, Modoc and Yahooskin: the 1864 treaty and termination (1954-1961) -- The 1864 treaty ceded land but kept hunting, fishing, trapping and gathering rights on reserved lands and waters (cession figures conflict: 'more than 6 million' vs 20 million acres; about 2 million acres retained). The tribes held about 862,622 acres after allotment and the largest remaining stand of ponderosa pine in the West. The Klamath Termination Act (Pub. L. 587, 68 Stat. 718, Aug. 13, 1954) let each adult member withdraw and receive the cash value of tribal property, with sales at appraised value; termination took effect in 1961. Of 2,133 members, 1,660 (78%) withdrew and received about $43,000 each. The Klamath Restoration Act (1986) re-established the Tribes but did not return the land base; the reservation today is 308 acres in twelve non-contiguous parcels. In 2002 a federal judge held (in United States v. Adair, filed 1975) that the Tribes' water rights predate those of non-tribal irrigators.
land_lost_description: Reservation and forest land base (to the forest sold or transferred); federal recognition 1961-1986.
acreage_if_known: 862,622 acres (post-allotment tribal holdings, Wikipedia); 308 acres today
legal_aftermath: Restored status (1986), land not restored; treaty hunting/fishing rights survived termination in practice (Kimball v. Callahan, 9th Cir. 1974 [from-memory]).
related_cases: United States v. Adair (D. Or. 2002; 9th Cir. 1983 [from-memory])

treaty_name: Treaty of Nation Ford (state treaty with South Carolina)
nations: Catawba Indian Nation
mechanism_summary: Catawba: South Carolina's 1840 Nation Ford treaty, never approved by the United States -- The Catawba sold all but one square mile of their 144,000-acre reserve to South Carolina under the 1840 treaty. The treaty never gained Senate ratification or federal approval, and the state lacked authority to make it (a power the Constitution gives the federal government; the Nonintercourse Act is the statutory bar). The federal government terminated the Catawba in 1959. The 1993 Settlement Act reversed termination, recognized the Catawba Indian Nation, and resolved land claims for $50 million with the state (3,000 acres [from-memory]).
land_lost_description: About 143,000 acres.
legal_aftermath: Claim resolved by settlement (1993) rather than by title recovery. South Carolina v. Catawba Indian Tribe, 476 U.S. 498 (1986) [from-memory] applied state limitations periods after termination.
related_cases: South Carolina v. Catawba Indian Tribe, Inc., 476 U.S. 498 (1986) [from-memory]

treaty_name: State of Massachusetts/Maine treaties with the Passamaquoddy, Penobscot and Maliseet (1794-1833)
nations: Passamaquoddy, Penobscot, Houlton Band of Maliseet
mechanism_summary: Maine: state treaties violating the Nonintercourse Act and the 1980 settlement -- The tribes' claim, litigated beginning in the 1970s, was that their land transfers to Massachusetts and Maine violated the Nonintercourse Act because Congress never approved them. The First Circuit's Passamaquoddy v. Morton (1975) recognized that the Act applied. The claim covered about 60% of Maine (Wikipedia's lead; other sources vary). The Maine Indian Claims Settlement Act (Pub. L. 96-420, signed Oct. 10, 1980) allocated $81.5 million and funds to buy up to 300,000 acres. In 2026 TPL-led and other transfers (e.g., about 11,000 acres to the Penobscot Nation in the first phase of a nearly 30,000-acre project, Sept. 17, 2026; about 3,400 acres to the Mi'kmaq Nation, June 2026) continue the process.
land_lost_description: Most of the aboriginal territory of the Wabanaki nations in Maine.
acreage_if_known: claim covered about 60% of Maine; settlement funded up to 300,000 acres
