legal_aftermath: Settlement 1980 (claims extinguished); the settlement's effect on tribal sovereignty remains contested [from-memory].
related_cases: Joint Tribal Council of Passamaquoddy Tribe v. Morton, 528 F.2d 370 (1st Cir. 1975)

treaty_name: 1825 and 1846 land agreements
nations: Kaw Nation (Kanza)
mechanism_summary: Kaw (Kanza): annuities delayed, sale and removal from Kansas (1873), and Kaw Lake -- In 1825 the Kaw ceded a large area of Missouri and Kansas for an annuity of $3,500 a year for twenty years, which was often delayed or diverted. In 1846 they sold most of their roughly 2,000,000 acres for $202,000, keeping a 256,000-acre reservation centered on Council Grove; it was cut to 80,000 acres in 1860. On June 4, 1873 the Kaw left Kansas for Indian Territory (533 people reached Kay County, Oklahoma). In 1902 Congress ended tribal government and the reservation and allotted 405 acres to each of 247 members; by 1945 members owned only about 13% of the former reservation. Kaw Lake (1960s) flooded the Washunga Council House and cemetery.
land_lost_description: Kansas homeland, then the Oklahoma land base; sacred sites at Washunga.
legal_aftermath: In 2000 the Nation bought land near Council Grove for the Allegawaho Memorial Heritage Park, dedicated June 19, 2005, a small return of presence to Kansas.

treaty_name: Treaty of Cession of Russian Possessions (1867), Art. III; no U.S.-Native treaties in Alaska
nations: Alaska Native peoples (Iñupiat, Yup'ik, Aleut/Unangan, Athabascan, Tlingit, Haida, Tsimshian, and others)
mechanism_summary: Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (1971): extinguishment of aboriginal title by statute -- Article III of the 1867 cession treaty stated that 'the uncivilized tribes will be subject to such laws and regulations as the United States may, from time to time, adopt' and did not recognize their title. In Tee-Hit-Ton Indians v. United States (Feb. 7, 1955) the Court held that taking unrecognized Indian title is not compensable under the Fifth Amendment. ANCSA (Pub. L. 92-203, Dec. 18, 1971) was a negotiated settlement: Sec. 4(b) extinguished all aboriginal titles and claims based on use and occupancy in Alaska, including submerged lands and 'any aboriginal hunting or fishing rights'; Sec. 4(c) extinguished claims against the United States, the State and others. In return: $462.5 million from the Treasury plus $500 million from mineral revenue sharing ($962.5 million), and about 40 million acres (38 million in Secs. 12(b)-(c) plus 2 million in Sec. 14(h); Wikipedia says up to 44 million), delivered to 12 regional corporations plus a 13th and over 200 village corporations. Congress declared the settlement should be 'without establishing any permanent racially defined institutions, rights, privileges, or obligations' and without a reservation system.
land_lost_description: Aboriginal-title and use-and-occupancy claims across the rest of Alaska (statewide land area is about 365 million acres [from-memory]) and aboriginal hunting and fishing rights as such.
legal_aftermath: ANCSA lands continue to be transferred (e.g., nearly 28,000 acres to NANA Regional Corporation in 2025-26); a new law removed a requirement that some land be held in state trust for a future village corporation (HCN 2026). Subsistence protection later came through ANILCA (1980) [from-memory].
related_cases: Tee-Hit-Ton Indians v. United States, 348 U.S. 272 (1955); Alaska v. Native Village of Venetie Tribal Government, 522 U.S. 520 (1998) (decided Feb. 25, 1998) [verified]

treaty_name: Treaty of Friendship, Commerce and Navigation (1849), 9 Stat. 977 (U.S.-Kingdom of Hawaii); not a treaty with a Native nation within the U.S.
nations: Kanaka Maoli (Native Hawaiians); Kingdom of Hawaii (sovereign state)
mechanism_summary: Hawaii (context): overthrow of the Kingdom (1893), annexation (1898) and the 1993 Apology -- LEGAL CATEGORY NOTE: the Kingdom of Hawaii was an internationally recognized state that signed treaties with the United States, e.g., the Dec. 20, 1849 treaty of friendship, commerce and navigation. The 1993 Apology Resolution (Pub. L. 103-150, Nov. 23, 1993) 'apologizes to Native Hawaiians on behalf of the people of the United States for the overthrow of the Kingdom of Hawaii on January 17, 1893 with the participation of agents and citizens of the United States.' A treaty of annexation signed in 1897 lacked the two-thirds Senate support; Congress instead annexed Hawaii by joint resolution (the Newlands Resolution, 30 Stat. 750): House 209-91 (June 15, 1898), Senate 42-21 (July 6, 1898), signed July 7, 1898. A 1897 petition against annexation gathered 21,269 signatures, more than half of the roughly 39,000 Native Hawaiians. The Territory was created in 1900. The resolution disclaims: 'Nothing in this Joint Resolution is intended to serve as a settlement of any claims against the United States.'
land_lost_description: Sovereignty and the Crown/government lands (acreage not verified).
legal_aftermath: Hawaii v. Office of Hawaiian Affairs (Mar. 31, 2009, unanimous, Alito): the Apology Resolution's apology and acknowledgment clauses are non-binding, do not create enforceable rights, and do not strip Hawaii's power to sell or transfer the ceded lands granted to the State at statehood.
related_cases: Hawaii v. Office of Hawaiian Affairs, 556 U.S. 163 (2009)

treaty_name: No treaty claim; Antiquities Act proclamations; Navajo (1868) and Ute (1868) treaties are historical context
nations: Hopi Tribe, Navajo Nation, Ute Mountain Ute Tribe, Ute Indian Tribe of the Uintah and Ouray Reservation, Pueblo of Zuni (Bears Ears Inter-Tribal Coalition)
mechanism_summary: Bears Ears National Monument (2016-2026): designation, reductions, restoration and the July 2026 action (context, not a treaty claim) -- Proclamation 9558 (Dec. 28, 2016) designated 1,351,849 acres; Proclamation 9681 (Dec. 4, 2017) reduced it to about 201,000 acres (removing more than 1.1 million acres); Proclamation 10285 (Oct. 8, 2021; 86 FR 57321) restored about 1.36 million acres and re-established the Bears Ears Commission to reflect 'expertise and traditional and historical knowledge of Tribal Nations.' On July 13, 2026 President Trump signed Proclamation 11043 (91 FR 45169, published July 17), which modified the monument's boundaries: reserved lands about 121,096 acres, about 1,238,904 acres excluded, Bears Ears Commission disbanded, excluded lands open to mineral and mining entry 60 days after signing. Native News Online's 'revoked' overstates it; Wikipedia's 'Proclamation 9558' label is wrong (9558 is the 2016 designation). High Country News and Courthouse News (91%) match the text. Legal challenge: NARF (for the Hopi, Zuni, Ute Mountain Ute) argues the Antiquities Act authorizes designation but not revocation; a suit by Patagonia, Hopi, Navajo, Ute Indian Tribe, Zuni and NRDC-led groups was reopened Sept. 2, 2026 before Judge Tanya Chutkan in D.D.C.; the Tenth Circuit in June 2026 affirmed in part, vacated in part and remanded challenges to the 2021 boundaries (per Wikipedia).
land_lost_description: Federal protection for cultural landscapes; the first tribal co-management commission.
acreage_if_known: 1.36 million acres (2021 boundary); post-July 2026 reserved acreage 121,096 (Proclamation 11043); 1,238,904 acres excluded
legal_aftermath: Pending litigation as of Oct. 2026.
related_cases: Hopi Tribe v. Trump (D.D.C.) [2017 filing; docket not confirmed]
